claims.text: A machine-learning interatomic potential combined with perturbative thermodynamic integration can faithfully reproduce solid and liquid free energies at fusion conditions.
The proposed hybrid framework can retain vibrational, anharmonic, and electron-vibration contributions to the free energy.
Replacing explicit ab initio molecular dynamics with the hybrid framework will substantially reduce computational cost.
Elemental metals and binary alloys such as pure Ni and Ni-Co have previously been validated for this methodological approach.
The approach can be extended from elemental and binary systems to multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
A training set containing anharmonic distortions and electron-vibration features will allow the ML potential to represent those effects.
Post-hoc thermodynamic-integration or free-energy-perturbation corrections can recover otherwise missing entropic contributions.
Vibrational, anharmonic, and electron-vibration effects are significant over approximately 1000-3000 K.
Local atomic environments and short-range order in the relevant disordered high-temperature phases can be adequately represented by the proposed training set.
ML interatomic potentials can reproduce DFT energies and forces with near-DFT accuracy in elemental and multicomponent systems.
An MTP for multicomponent MoNbTaW achieved energy mean absolute errors of about 4.3-4.6 meV per atom on test and training data.
Thermodynamic integration in the proposed framework will recover vibrational, anharmonic, and electronic entropy contributions.
Vibrational free energy can materially change phase stability at elevated temperature.
The hybrid method will predict fusion free energies and transition observables within approximately 5-10 meV per atom of explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics results.
The hybrid method will be 10-100 times faster than DFT-based molecular dynamics.
The hybrid method will be competitive with or faster than TOR-TILD for multicomponent systems.
The method is expected to remain valid for FCC or BCC high-temperature disordered alloys containing five or more elements.
Strong chemical or magnetic ordering, particularly significantly below 1000 K, may increase the method's errors.
Complete solid and liquid free-energy curves, transition temperatures, and entropy contributions can decisively benchmark the method against explicit ab initio MD and TOR-TILD.
